issues.claim: §3 + §5: 'For us: if SFT lands at 40–70%, plan on +10 to +20 points in sim', with the §3 table as support. The chosen §5 method is 'iterative filtered BC with sim-expert corrections'.
issues.problem: This is overstated, and it is the biggest flaw in the doc. Every row of the §3 table comes from true online RL with exploration: SimpleVLA-RL uses GRPO with a binary 0/1 outcome reward, πRL uses PPO/GRPO via Flow-Noise/Flow-SDE, RL4VLA uses PPO (and found PPO beats DPO/GRPO), and VLA-RL uses online RL. The §5 method is something else: keep the successes, add scripted-expert corrections, and run BC again. That is self-imitation plus automated DAgger, and nothing in the table measures its gain. Ilia's own method, AWR plus RECAP advantage conditioning, is also not PPO, and he reports no RL-vs-BC number either. So the +10 to +20 forecast borrows gains from a different algorithm family.
issues.fix: Call §5 what it is: 'filtered BC + scripted-expert DAgger (not RL)'. Either drop the +10–20 forecast or label it [I, no direct evidence for this method]. If a real RL number is wanted, use RLinf π0.5 PPO (see the RLinf issue) and say the §3 numbers apply only to that branch. Keep the matched 'more SFT steps' control. It is the only thing that will show whether the loop adds anything.
issues.evidence: SimpleVLA-RL uses a binary reward and GRPO: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.09674. πRL uses PPO/GRPO on flow VLAs: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.25889v3. RL4VLA (PPO > GRPO/DPO): https://arxiv.org/html/2505.19789v4. Ilia, arXiv 2606.27163 §1: 'engineering case study, not a controlled experiment ... little formal ablations'.

issues.claim: §3: 'The real robot: every sim-to-real RL result used a photoreal twin (RLB).'
issues.problem: This is false. RL4VLA Appendix B.4 retrained SFT and RL policies in ManiSkill with the camera views aligned and deployed them zero-shot on a real Franka. Pick-and-place went from SFT 0.00 to RL 0.27, and grasp from 0.10 to 0.43, over 30 trials, with no photoreal twin mentioned. SimpleVLA-RL trained in RoboTwin 2.0 sim only and deployed on real AgileX Piper arms. Its average went from 17.5% (SFT) to 38.5% (RL), with Click Bell 30 → 60 and Stack Bowls 38 → 70.
issues.fix: Replace it with: 'Sim-trained RL has transferred zero-shot in two papers (RL4VLA: real Franka pick-place 0% → 27%; SimpleVLA-RL: real Piper 17.5% → 38.5% average). Absolute real success stayed low, and neither used our robot.' The 'Will not claim real-robot success' line still stands.
issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.19789v4 (Appendix B.4); https://arxiv.org/html/2509.09674 (sim-to-real table)

issues.claim: §3: 'Genuinely new situations: RL sharpens behaviour it has already seen, and Ilia's recoveries came only from human intervention [V].' Also 'Gains are large when SFT is weak and small when it is already good.'
issues.problem: This takes one method family and states it as a general rule. Ilia does say this (§10.4), but he says it about his own AWR/RECAP plus CFG plus best-of-N, which never explores. Outcome-reward RL with exploration has found behaviour that was not in the demos: SimpleVLA-RL's 'pushcut', where the policy learned to push instead of grasp. RL4VLA also contradicts the 'weak SFT only' framing. Its SFT used 16k demos and was already strong (78.1% in distribution), yet RL gave large out-of-distribution execution gains: unseen robot init pose 33.9 → 79.7 and mid-episode object reposition 28.6 → 74.5.
issues.fix: Scope the sentence: 'Reweighting/filtering methods (Ilia's AWR+RECAP, our filtered BC) only sharpen behaviour already present. Exploring RL (PPO/GRPO) can find new strategies and gives its largest gains on execution shifts even from strong SFT.' This is also the honest answer to the owner's 'what does RL add' question.
issues.evidence: Ilia §10.4 'The proposed RL approach is great at reproducing and sharpening behavior it has seen': arXiv 2606.27163. Pushcut: https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09674. RL4VLA Table 1, Appendix B.3: https://arxiv.org/html/2505.19789v4

issues.claim: §5: 'Out of scope: RLinf PPO (ROCm support is claimed but unshown on MI300X; wrapping our env is ~0.5–1 day).'
issues.problem: This is out of date. The RLinf README's hardware matrix marks π₀/π₀.₅ (OpenPI) on LIBERO and ManiSkill as supported on AMD ROCm. It ships a container, rlinf/rlinf:agentic-rlinf0.4-maniskill_libero-rocm7.2, built with ROCM_ARCHS=gfx90a;gfx942, and gfx942 is the MI300X. It also documents the same CPU OSMesa rendering we would need (MUJOCO_GL=osmesa). RLinf's own blog (updated 2026-09-21) ran RL on 'one node with eight AMD MI300-series GPUs ... ROCm 6.4 ... 84–116 GB out of 192 GB'. That run was OpenVLA-OFT GRPO in a world model. No public π0.5 PPO benchmark numbers on MI300X were found, so 'unbenchmarked' is fair. 'Unshown on MI300X' is not.
issues.fix: Reword to: 'RLinf officially supports π0.5 on ROCm with a gfx942 image, and RLinf has run RL on MI300-series. π0.5 PPO throughput on MI300X is unbenchmarked.' Promote the reserved ≤2 h RLinf LIBERO smoke test to an early go/no-go. If it passes, real PPO becomes a feasible §5 branch, with the env wrapping still costing ~0.5–1 day.
issues.evidence: https://github.com/RLinf/RLinf (README 'Hardware Support' table and the 2026/08 news line); docs/source-en/rst_source/examples/embodied/_amd_libero.rst and _libero_osmesa.rst; docs/source-en/rst_source/resources/blog/worldloop_topreward.rst line 143

issues.problem: LeRobot 0.6.2 does not exist. The latest release on PyPI and GitHub is v0.6.1 (2026-08-03), after v0.6.0 (2026-07-06). The torch pin is correct: torch<2.12.0,>=2.7.

issues.claim: Context and §8: 'Optional comparison: VLA-JEPA (reportedly in LeRobot 0.6; unverified).'
issues.problem: This can now be marked verified. VLA-JEPA shipped in LeRobot v0.6.0 as policy type vla_jepa (src/lerobot/policies/vla_jepa exists at tag v0.6.1). It is built on Qwen3-VL-2B with V-JEPA2 latent-future supervision during training only, and the checkpoints include lerobot/VLA-JEPA-Pretrain (DROID) and lerobot/VLA-JEPA-LIBERO. The same release added Robometer (Qwen3-VL-4B) and TOPReward (zero-shot) to a unified reward API. 'TOPReward-8B' is not a released model: TOPReward is a method applied to an off-the-shelf VLM (RLinf used Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct).
issues.fix: Mark VLA-JEPA, Robometer and TOPReward as [V], available in lerobot 0.6.1. Write the contender as 'TOPReward on Qwen3-VL-8B'. Note that VLA-JEPA is a cheap and honest way to have 'JEPA' in the training stack, beside the judge.

issues.claim: §2: 'Use V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L instead if torch.hub loads it; its weights licence is unstated [V].'
issues.problem: torch.hub will not load the pretrained weights from main for either V-JEPA 2 or 2.1. src/hub/backbones.py sets VJEPA_BASE_URL = "http://localhost:8300", with the dl.fbaipublicfiles.com line commented out. On licence: the repo's GitHub licence is MIT, and the README says 'The majority of V-JEPA 2 is licensed under MIT'. The 2.1 checkpoints are linked from that README with no separate terms, so 'unstated' really means 'not separately stated'. The HF V-JEPA 2 ViT-L (facebook/vjepa2-vitl-fpc64-256) is tagged MIT, which is correct. V-JEPA 2.1 checkpoints are 384 px, which is heavier per clip than the 256 px V-JEPA 2.
issues.fix: Download the 2.1 .pt directly from dl.fbaipublicfiles.com/vjepa2/ and load the state dict, or patch VJEPA_BASE_URL. Record the licence as 'repo MIT; checkpoints carry no separate terms'. Keep the HF V-JEPA 2 ViT-L as the default.
issues.evidence: https://github.com/facebookresearch/vjepa2 (README License section; src/hub/backbones.py line 11); https://huggingface.co/facebook/vjepa2-vitl-fpc64-256 (license: mit)

issues.claim: §2 Precedent: 'arXiv 2510.16240 used a frozen V-JEPA 2 with a 4-block probe ... ICC 0.836 against humans, where human–human agreement was 0.811 [V].'
issues.problem: The numbers check out. The configuration does not match ours. The paper is Cosmos-Surg-dVRK: a frozen V-JEPA 2 ViT-H (~632M) with a 4-block attentive probe (~77M trainable). It was trained on 2,310 hand-labelled 32-frame clips with 3 classes (Success/Anomaly/Default), and it scored surgical (dVRK) rollouts generated by a world model. ICC(2,1) was 0.836 against humans versus 0.811 human-human. Our plan uses ViT-L, 16-frame chunks and labels from sim state.
issues.fix: Cite it as 'ViT-H, 32-frame clips, ~2.3k human labels, surgical world-model video'. Treat the ViT-L/16-frame choice as a deviation to test, for example by also running the ViT-H probe if time allows.
issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2510.16240v2 (Sec. 3.2, 5.2, App. A.1, Table 4)

issues.claim: §6: 'MimicGen's generation rate fell from 73.7% to 60.9% at 5 mm pose noise.'
issues.problem: Correct as far as it goes, but cherry-picked. That is Square D0 at noise Level 1, which is 5 mm plus 5° of rotation noise. Other tasks fell much further at the same level: Coffee D0 78.2 → 28.9 and Threading D0 51.0 → 17.6. Level 2 (10 mm, 10°) took Square to 30.5. Meanwhile the success of policies trained on the generated data barely moved (Square 90.7 → 89.3 → 84.7). So pose noise mainly costs generation yield, not policy quality.
issues.fix: Report it as: 'At 5 mm/5° noise MimicGen's yield fell 13–49 points depending on the task, while downstream policy success held. With our physics verifier as the filter, calibration error costs yield more than it costs quality.'
issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2310.17596 (appendix on pose-estimation noise)

issues.claim: §6 Units: 'Convert with q_rad = sign·deg2rad(v) + off, starting from sign +1, off 0' ... 'Pass: offsets within 1–2°.'
issues.problem: Degrees mode is confirmed. RANGE_M100_100 clamps to [min,max] and so maps to [−100,100], while DEGREES does not clamp, and the dataset shows lift −105.7, wrist_flex 103.5 and wrist_roll 134.2. But the zero point needs stating. In LeRobot, deg = (raw − (range_min+range_max)/2)·360/4095. So 0° is the midpoint of the range of motion recorded at calibration. The exception is wrist_roll, whose range is forced to 0–4095, so its 0° is the hand-placed homing pose. off=0 is a sound prior only because Menagerie's so101 comes from so101_new_calib, whose 'virtual zero is set to the middle of its joint range'. The dataset already goes past Menagerie's limits: shoulder_lift −105.7° against ±100°, and wrist_flex 103.5° against ±95°. That implies offsets or range mismatches of ≥5.7–8.5°, or clipping on replay, which the verifier will reject as a limit violation. A 1–2° pass criterion is unlikely for lift and wrist_flex.
issues.fix: Make the friend's calibration JSON (homing_offset, range_min, range_max) the primary source. Compute each joint's offset as the gap between that arm's recorded mid-range and the model's joint-limit mid-range. Use the table-plane fit only as a cross-check. Count replayed real frames that exceed the MJCF limits before seeding. Treat the wrist_roll offset and the gripper map (RANGE_0_100, linear between recorded min and max) as per-arm values derived from the JSON.
issues.evidence: lerobot v0.6.1 src/lerobot/motors/motors_bus.py _normalize (lines 867–877); src/lerobot/robots/so_follower/so_follower.py calibrate() (wrist_roll range 0..4095; use_degrees=True default); https://github.com/TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100/blob/main/Simulation/SO101/README.md; Menagerie so101.xml joint ranges; dataset meta/stats.json at https://huggingface.co/datasets/MinhDuk/final_dataset_annotated

issues.claim: §4 Ilia: 'first checkpoint worth 0.5, paid gradually as the collar–sleeve gap closes'; 'on-policy Isaac Sim rollouts'; 'an advantage token'; 'Real round: plain BC + DAgger'.
issues.problem: The core is verified: the binary geometric success, six check_points read from the cloth mesh, the 0.5/1.0 checkpoints, withdrawal on failure so the return equals 1[success], no PPO, GAE with γ 0.999 and λ 0.99 from the success and completion heads, frame sampling ∝ exp(clip(A,−2,2)), CFG 7–9, best-of-2–3, 20k BC warm-up, and 79.63% vs 73.50%. Four details are off. (a) Only tops get the gradual 0.5, tied to the 'primary proximity distance'. Long pants get a spike checkpoint and short pants get none. (b) The rollouts are asynchronous and reuse stale data: each rollout set decays 0.98 per iteration, and the advantage blends toward a GRPO-style outcome baseline as data ages. That is not strictly on-policy. (c) Advantage conditioning enters through the prefix and through AdaRMS in the action expert, not only as a token. (d) The real policy was fine-tuned from a late, RL-trained sim checkpoint with sim success replays and intervention-weighted sampling, so it was not 'plain BC'. The checker also has '>= thr' spread conditions, not just proximity ones.
issues.fix: Correct these four phrases. Note that RL may have reached the real round indirectly, through the starting checkpoint and the replays.
issues.evidence: arXiv 2606.27163: §6.1 ('Gradual first checkpoint (applied to tops only)'), §6.4–6.5, §7.3, §9 and Table 6; organizer checker check_top_sleeve/check_pant_* (p[0..5], <= and >= conditions)

issues.claim: §7 step 6: 'Stop if round 1 gains < ~7 pts (95% CI, n=200)'; §2 gate 'AUC ≥0.95 and at least 0.02 above the best zero-shot model' with '≈±0.03 AUC'.
issues.problem: The ±7 points is the 95% CI of a single success rate (p≈0.5, n=200). The CI of a difference between two independent rates at n=200 each is about ±9.6 points (for example 0.55 vs 0.62), so a 7-point gain is not significant. For the AUC, Hanley–McNeil at AUC 0.95 with 200/200 gives SE ≈0.011, a CI of about ±0.022. A 0.02 margin is therefore inside the noise unless it is tested with a paired test.
issues.fix: Evaluate both policies on the same 200 seeds and use McNemar (paired), or raise n to about 400 per arm. State the minimum detectable gain honestly (~10 points). For the judge, use a paired DeLong test on the shared clips.
issues.evidence: Standard binomial and Hanley–McNeil (1982) formulas; arithmetic: 1.96·sqrt(.55·.45/200 + .62·.38/200) ≈ 0.096

issues.claim: §7: 'Snapshot and destroy the droplet when idle; a powered-off droplet may still bill [?]'.
issues.problem: AMD Developer Cloud GPU droplets run on DigitalOcean. DigitalOcean documents that powered-off GPU droplets keep billing because the GPU stays reserved, and billing ends only on destroy. Snapshots are billed separately per GB-month. AMD's own policy was not found, but the underlying platform is clear.
issues.fix: Change it to: 'Powered-off still bills (DigitalOcean); always snapshot then destroy.' Check one hour of the billing dashboard after the first destroy.
issues.evidence: https://docs.digitalocean.com/products/droplets/details/pricing/

issues.claim: §4 guards: 'The both-jaw clause blocks pushing instead of grasping (SimpleVLA-RL's "pushcut")'; milestone '+0.1 ... (the RL4VLA/πRL value)'.
issues.problem: Small attribution errors. SimpleVLA-RL presents pushcut as a useful new strategy that outcome-only reward discovered, not as reward hacking. Our both-jaw clause legitimately rules it out because the task requires a grasp, but 'gaming' misstates the source. RL4VLA's reward is '0.1 for grasping and continuously holding the correct object, 1.0 for placing'. It has no 0.5 s lift condition and no withdrawal on failure. The πRL attribution was not verified.
issues.fix: Say 'pushcut (SimpleVLA-RL's emergent push strategy) is excluded by task definition', and cite the 0.1 to RL4VLA only.
issues.evidence: https://arxiv.org/html/2509.09674; https://arxiv.org/html/2505.19789v4 (reward section)

issues.claim: §6: '5 DoF allows top-down grasps only'; co-training 'in real units and camera keys'.
issues.problem: Minor. A 5-DoF SO-101 (pan, lift, elbow, wrist_flex, wrist_roll) restricts the approach direction to the vertical plane through the base axis, but the pitch within that plane is free. So angled grasps are possible, not only top-down ones. Also, the friend's dataset has exactly two cameras, observation.images.cam_head and cam_right, with no wrist camera, so a sim co-training set must match those two keys. Separately, π0.5 weights (lerobot/pi05_base) are under the Gemma licence, which carries over to fine-tuned checkpoints you publish.
issues.fix: Reword to 'approach direction limited to the radial vertical plane'. Fix sim camera keys to cam_head/cam_right. Add the Gemma licence to the model card in step 8.
issues.evidence: https://huggingface.co/datasets/MinhDuk/final_dataset_annotated/resolve/main/meta/info.json; https://huggingface.co/lerobot/pi05_base (license: gemma)

issues.claim: §7: the build plan fits in ~40 droplet-hours (2+4+3+10+1.5+10+5+1+3.5). Snapshot and destroy the droplet when idle; a powered-off droplet may still bill [?].
issues.problem: The 40 hours are wall-clock time, not busy time, and the clock is already running. The droplet was created at ~08:57 UTC on 9 Oct. The owner's droplet rules set a hard stop at 40 alive hours and forbid snapshots, because snapshots bill his card. The window therefore closes at ~00:57 UTC on Sun 11 Oct (07:57 Hanoi), about 39.5 h from the time of this review. The table assumes 40 busy hours with zero idle time. Laptop step L, sleep, discussion and debugging all burn the same clock. The sequential GPU critical path 1→2→4→5→6→8 is already 28.5 h, and step 7 (5 h) shares the same single GPU. The missing items in the issues below add 8–20 h, so the plan overruns, and the wall will cut it off in the middle of RL.
issues.evidence: video2sim-so101/CLAUDE.md: 'Hard stop at 40 alive hours total', 'Do NOT use DigitalOcean snapshots or backups'. HANDOFF.md: 'created at about 08:57 UTC on 9 Oct'. Powered-off droplets still bill (DigitalOcean community answer): https://www.digitalocean.com/community/questions/when-a-droplet-is-stopped-does-it-incur-only-the-storage-cost-or-vm-cost-too
issues.fix: Re-plan against the wall clock and put the one long unattended job (SFT) overnight. Example: Fri 09:30–11:30 UTC, render A/B, tokenizer check and pi05 smoke test. 11:30–13:00, datagen of 300 sugar episodes plus negatives, LeRobotDataset load and HF push. Fri 13:00 to Sat 00:00 UTC, SFT unattended with HF checkpoints every 30 min; meanwhile V-JEPA features and the eval harness. Sat 00–02, eval. Sat 02–09, one filtered-BC round plus the control. Sat 09–13, package. Destroy at ~Sat 14:00 UTC: about 29 alive hours with ~11 h slack. Replace the '[?] powered-off may bill' line with 'powered-off bills; snapshots forbidden; destroy only when finished'.

issues.claim: Step 2: datagen of ~1,000 episodes plus 400 judge clips on CPU in 4 h. Step 1: 'measure render fps in hour one' via OSMesa/EGL.
issues.problem: Render speed was already measured on this droplet, and the result is far below the plan. Only OSMesa works there; EGL failed. 20 episodes on 16 workers took more than 6 minutes, with a load average of ~52 on 20 vCPUs. That is ~0.03–0.055 episodes/s, so 1,000 sugar episodes take ~5–9 h and the judge clips another 1–3 h. By my arithmetic the upper bound is ~0.2–0.34 CPU-s per 256² frame. The causes are visible in the code. MuJoCo's defaults are shadowsize=4096 and offsamples=4 (checked on mujoco 3.11.0): a 16.8M-pixel shadow pass per frame, about 64× the main pass, plus 4× MSAA. scene.py adds a key light with castshadow=True and table reflectance 0.05, which costs an extra mirrored pass. llvmpipe also defaults to one thread per core in every process, which oversubscribes the CPUs. EGL could never have helped: CDNA3 has no raster hardware, so it would be llvmpipe either way.
issues.evidence: video2sim-so101/HANDOFF.md (09:11 UTC notes: 'roughly 20 episodes in 6+ minutes ... N=1000 at about 5 hours', 'Load average is about 52'). CLAUDE.md: 'EGL fails here'. Project memory: '0.03 eps/s on OSMesa'. r2s/scene.py lines 87–92. Mesa llvmpipe docs (threads default to the core count, up to 32): https://docs.mesa3d.org/drivers/llvmpipe.html. CDNA has no ROPs or rasterizer: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CDNA_(microarchitecture)
issues.fix: Before any large run, A/B one episode at a time: LP_NUM_THREADS=1 with 19 workers; shadowsize 1024, or castshadow off on training cameras with shadows kept only for the hero video; offsamples 0–1; reflectance 0; render 224×224 (π0.5's input size) instead of 256; optionally render at 10 Hz and repeat each image for 3 frames, keeping 30 Hz state and action. Gate at ≥0.5 episodes/s. Even with no fix, 300 episodes take 1.5–2.8 h, so cut N to 300 (see the SFT issue).

issues.claim: Step 4: π0.5 SFT for 10 h on the ~1,000-episode dataset.
issues.problem: The only published per-step anchor for pi05 is 2.548 s/step at batch 32 per H100 (gradient checkpointing, bf16, full fine-tune), about 12.6 samples/s per GPU. On MI300X with ROCm eager PyTorch I assume [I] 0.6–1.1× of that. Ten hours then gives ~270k–500k samples, or ~8–16k steps at batch 32. The 1,000 sugar episodes hold 523k frames (synthetic: 915k), so SFT covers less than one epoch, while LeRobot's guide says imitation learning converges in 5–10 epochs. Two thirds of the rendered frames would never be trained on, which wastes 3–6 alive hours. The LeRobot pi05 defaults are also wrong for this run: dtype=float32, scheduler_decay_steps=30,000 (the learning rate stays near peak at 10k steps) and eager attention.
issues.evidence: LeRobot hardware guide (4×H100 table: pi05 3h41m, update_s 2.548, batch 32; 'converges in 5–10 epochs'): https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/en/hardware_guide. pi05 configuration defaults: https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/blob/main/src/lerobot/policies/pi05/configuration_pi05.py. Datagen README: 523 frames per sugar episode, 915 per synthetic.
issues.fix: Generate ~300 sugar episodes (~157k frames, 2–3 epochs in 10 h). Pass --policy.dtype=bfloat16 and set scheduler_decay_steps to the planned step count. Measure s/step with gradient_checkpointing=false, which 192 GB allows, in a 20-step smoke test. Leave compile_model off unless it measurably helps on ROCm. Shorten episodes (robot_time_scale, the 0.5 s rest), because every frame costs rendering and training. Decide steps = 10 h ÷ measured s/step before launching.

issues.claim: §5: rollouts run at 1–3 episodes/s [I], 2,000 per round, rendering only when the policy is queried.
issues.problem: There are three gaps. (a) Filtered BC trains on the kept rollouts, so every frame of every kept episode needs images. Re-rendering ~1,000 successes per round is ~1.05M frames, about 3–5 h per round at the measured speed, and it is not budgeted. (b) 1–3 episodes/s needs a batched inference server or ~8 concurrent bf16 replicas. Batch-1 π0.5 latency is 76 ms even on an RTX 4090 with openpi/JAX and 5 denoising steps, and 130–165 ms on a LeRobot port. LeRobot pi05 defaults to fp32 with eager attention. A 17 s episode needs 11–18 chunk queries (n_action_steps=50), so sequential rollouts run at ~0.1–0.3 episodes/s, and replanning every 10 frames is 5× worse. (c) The plan contradicts itself: step 5 budgets 1.5 h for 400 eval episodes (~0.07 episodes/s), while step 6 assumes 1–3 episodes/s. At 0.07 episodes/s, two rounds of 2,000 rollouts take 16 h of rollouts alone.
issues.evidence: pi05 defaults (chunk_size 50, n_action_steps 50, num_inference_steps 10, dtype float32). modeling_pi05.py: 'eager by default'. Real-time chunking paper (π0.5, 4090, bf16, 5 steps = 76 ms): https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07339. π0 at 73 ms on a 4090: https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164
issues.fix: In the smoke test, measure bf16 inference latency at batch 1 and batch 8–16. Size the round as N = hours × measured episodes/s; plan on one round of ~500. Run 4–8 rollout processes, each with its own bf16 replica (~7 GB each), instead of building a batched server. Re-render only the successes, at 224 px and 10 Hz with held frames, and give that its own budget line.

issues.claim: Build table: steps 5 and 6 (eval and RL) can run once SFT finishes. Step L lists only calibration, the failure injector, the real-unit writer and expert restart.
issues.problem: The policy-in-the-loop harness is missing as a line item, and steps 5 and 6 both depend on it. It has to load pi05, run CPU MuJoCo with the verifier on every step, render on query, map joint units, run 200 paired seeds and handle the perturbation axes. datagen/rollout.py is tied to the scripted expert. The plan's own note puts a comparable RLinf env wrap at 0.5–1 day. Expert restart from arbitrary failure states is a second unbudgeted build, marked [?].
issues.evidence: final_design.md §5 ('wrapping our env is ~0.5–1 day') and §7 table. datagen README: the planner re-plans only at 3 fixed stage points.
issues.fix: Add 'eval/rollout harness' as an explicit task. Write it on spare CPUs during the overnight SFT and test it on an intermediate checkpoint. Cut expert-restart corrections this weekend and use plain filtered BC.

issues.claim: Step 6: RL in 10 h for 2 rounds. Control: continue SFT on the original demos for the same number of steps.
issues.problem: The control arm doubles each round's fine-tune GPU time and is not in the table. Neither is the re-render. Each round's ~3 h fine-tune (~130k samples) also covers only ~0.25 epoch of the 523k frames from 1,000 kept rollouts. A realistic estimate is 2 × (rollouts 0.5–3 h + re-render 0.5–5 h + fine-tune 3 h + eval 0.5 h) + control 6 h ≈ 15–29 h, against 10 h budgeted.
issues.evidence: Arithmetic from the SFT and rollout issues above. final_design.md §7.
issues.fix: Run one round of ~500 rollouts. Fine-tune both the RL arm and the control with --policy.train_expert_only=true: this freezes the 2B VLM, which makes the backward pass cheaper [I]. Run the two arms concurrently on the 192 GB card after a memory check, with the same steps and the same eval seeds.

issues.claim: Gate: stop if round 1 gains less than ~7 points (95% CI, n=200).

MuJoCo segmentation rendering gives the cube's pixel count per camera per frame, and frustum projection catches bad camera draws. A learned judge is strictly worse at this. (b) Ranking real episodes means applying a sim-trained probe to real video, which §2's own 'Not used for' list forbids. It also has no labels: every friend episode holds the cube for at least 1 s, so the episodes are curated successes, and a success probe's ranking among them reflects visual nuisance such as lighting. As designed, JEPA gates nothing in the engine, so 'dataset judged by JEPA' is not literally true.

issues.claim: §6 units/validation: the table-plane z-variance fit, rest pose, a homography from FK(x,y) to the cam_head centroid, and 'pass if offsets within 1–2°' are enough to avoid silent corruption.
issues.problem: Several unit errors would get through this validation unseen. A free 8-DoF homography absorbs both a shoulder_pan rotation offset and a pan sign flip (mirror), and the z-plane test is blind to pan entirely. wrist_roll errors of k·90° cannot be seen with a 4-fold-symmetric cube and a round bowl, so sim still passes. The friend's data has a wrist_roll mean of 76.6° and the so-frame −90° shift is arm-specific. In LeRobot DEGREES mode, zero is the midpoint of the min/max range the operator swept during calibration, so 'off 0' is a weak prior. Minimizing z variance over three coupled offsets with grasp-depth noise is poorly conditioned. And '1–2°' has no reference value to compare against. Once data is merged, mean/std normalization hides any unit mismatch: loss still falls while actions are wrong.
